claims.text: Processing a metallic alloy to form hierarchical, coherent second-phase precipitates within a ductile matrix can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off.
The designed precipitate architecture improves tensile strength relative to an equivalent conventionally processed single-phase material.
The designed precipitate architecture improves tensile ductility relative to an equivalent conventionally processed single-phase material.
The initial as-cast or homogenized alloy has a relatively coarse or uniform microstructure without specialized secondary phases.
Stepwise controlled thermal or mechanical processing can create multiscale coherent precipitates in a ductile matrix.
Forging is an applicable part of the processing route used to create the proposed precipitate architecture.
The proposed strength and ductility are obtained under ambient-temperature tensile testing.
A strain rate of approximately 10^-3 to 10^-4 s^-1 is a standard or applicable testing condition for the reported outcome.
The treatment nucleates fine-scale coherent secondary-phase precipitates within a ductile metallic matrix.
Coherent precipitates impede dislocation flow.
Impeded dislocation flow increases alloy strength.
Coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission between precipitate and matrix regions.
Dislocation transmission across coherent interfaces relieves stress concentrations and delays premature crack initiation.
Coherent interfaces delay crack propagation.
The coherent-interface mechanism increases tensile ductility.
Room-temperature yield strength can exceed 2 GPa.
Room-temperature tensile ductility can remain above approximately 10%.
The precipitate-designed alloy exceeds the strength and ductility of a comparable alloy lacking the designed architecture.
The effectiveness of the strategy depends on alloy composition, heat-treatment parameters, and precipitate scale.
Excessive precipitation or excessively large precipitates may reduce ductility.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that excessive precipitation may reduce ductility, whereas the falsification rule treats failure of higher precipitate densities to improve both properties as falsifying the hypothesis. A high-density sample could therefore satisfy the stated boundary condition while also triggering the stated falsification criterion.
